mioc-070.title: The Pisco Formation's marine treasures
mioc-070.text: Peru's Pisco Formation ranks among the most important Lagerstätten, fossil sites of exceptional preservation. Its desert rocks hold megalodon, penguins, whales, marine crocodiles and even aquatic sloths. Together they give a crowded, detailed record of the life along South America's Pacific coast, spanning millions of years.

mioc-090.title: The Qaidam Basin dries out
mioc-090.text: Rock weathers fastest where water is plentiful. Around 12.6 Ma, the weathering of silicate rock in China's Qaidam Basin fell sharply. The drop marks a major aridification event, the basin turning dry. It was one sign of the growing dryness that would spread across Asia and the world later in the Miocene.

mioc-100.title: The Benguela Upwelling begins
mioc-100.text: Off southwestern Africa, cold, nutrient-rich water began rising from the deep in the late Miocene. This Benguela Upwelling likely fed the phytoplankton behind the rich marine fossils of Hondeklip Bay. On land it had the opposite effect. Today the cold Benguela Current along the coast helps keep the Namib Desert arid.

mioc-102.title: Europe's big mammals decline
mioc-102.text: Europe's variety of large mammals fell significantly during the Late Miocene. The drying climate picked winners and losers. In Iberia, grazers diversified while browsers declined, as open grass replaced the leaves that browsing animals depended on.

mioc-103.title: South America's giant crocodilians vanish
mioc-103.text: Purussaurus, a caiman, was the largest of the Miocene crocodilians. It and the gharial Gryposuchus died out in the late Miocene. Their end probably came as northern South America's wetlands vanished, the swamps and lakes they had depended on.

mioc-104.title: The last sebecosuchians hang on in the Antilles
mioc-104.text: Sebecids were the last of the sebecosuchians, land-dwelling relatives of crocodiles. They apparently survived on the Greater Antilles until the late Miocene or early Pliocene, an island refuge for the final members of a long line.

mioc-106.title: South America's marsupial-like predators fade
mioc-106.text: For a long time, South America's top meat-eaters were sparassodonts, relatives of marsupials. From the Late Miocene they declined, possibly because of cooling. The borhyaenids, one of their families, are last known from the latest Miocene.

mioc-108.title: Danuvius, an ape that may have walked upright
mioc-108.text: In a clay pit in southern Germany lay the bones of Danuvius guggenmosi, a great ape dated to 11.62 million years ago. Its discoverer argues it both hung in trees and walked upright along branches. That 'extended limb clambering' may have come before human bipedalism. Other researchers disagree. They say the fragmentary remains differ too little from other fossil apes to show how upright walking began.

mioc-109.title: Lazarussuchus, last of the choristoderes
mioc-109.text: Choristoderes were semiaquatic reptiles dating back to the Middle Jurassic. They survived the extinction that killed the dinosaurs, then died out in the Miocene for unclear reasons. The last was Lazarussuchus, a European genus. Its last definite remains are Early Miocene, from the Czech Republic, with possible remains from about 11.6 Ma.

mioc-110.title: The Late Miocene Cool Interval begins
mioc-110.text: About 11 Ma, the Middle Miocene Warm Interval ended and the much cooler Late Miocene Cool Interval began. From here on, Earth's climate grew increasingly like today's. The cold hit some animals hard. Desmostylians, cold-adapted marine mammals, declined during the Middle to Late Miocene cooling, which may have been harsher than earlier cold spells. Their end comes in {{ref:mioc-143}}.

mioc-111.title: The modern Yangtze takes shape
mioc-111.text: The modern Yangtze River is estimated to have originated around 11 Ma. The evidence lies in the mud it carried. Sedimentation rates suggest that its present outlet to the sea is no older than the late Miocene, about 11 Ma.

mioc-112.title: A brief warm pulse at 10.8 Ma
mioc-112.text: The Late Miocene cooling did not run smoothly. Around 10.8–10.7 Ma, early in the Late Miocene, a major but short-lived warming broke the trend. Then the cooling resumed, with the climate drifting toward today's.

mioc-113.title: Aguas Calientes erupts the Tajamar ignimbrite
mioc-113.text: High in the Andes, the Aguas Calientes caldera erupted the Tajamar ignimbrite between 10.5 and 10.1 Ma. About 350 km³ of rock poured out. It was one of a long run of great eruptions in the Central Andes, the volcanism that had begun in {{ref:mioc-021}}.

mioc-114.title: Ancient Lake Idaho fills for the first time
mioc-114.text: Lake Idaho came and went. It existed in a first phase from about 10.1 to 6.4 Ma. Then it vanished, only to return from 4.3 to 2.5 Ma, filling the same region a second time.

mioc-116.title: The elephant family arises in Africa
mioc-116.text: Around 10 Ma, the first members of the elephant family, Elephantidae, arose in Africa from gomphotheres. They were part of a broader change. From the Late Miocene many proboscideans grew ever larger tusks and shorter lower jaws. Climate change drove other groups, such as amebelodontids and choerolophodontids, into decline and extinction. The first members of modern elephant genera appeared around 6–5 Ma, at the Miocene–Pliocene transition.

mioc-117.title: Greenland's rising edges make room for ice
mioc-117.text: Greenland's ice needed high ground. Around 10 Ma, Greenland's western margin began to rise, later forming plateaus 2,000–3,000 m high. The eastern uplands followed about 5 Ma. This uplift made a single, connected Greenland ice sheet possible. Greenland may have had large glaciers as early as 8–7 Ma, though forests survived there into the Pliocene.

mioc-118.title: Ground sloths island-hop to North America
mioc-118.text: Sloths reached North America before any land bridge. Megalonychid and mylodontid ground sloths had island-hopped north by about 10–9 Ma, using islands forming between the Americas. The earliest North American megalonychid, Pliometanastes, lived in the southern US about 9 Ma. Traffic may have gone both ways. Some large North American herbivores may have reached South America 10–9 Ma over an incomplete land bridge. These crossings were an early phase of the exchange described in {{ref:plio-057}}.

mioc-120.title: Ten-million-year-old apes of East Africa
mioc-120.text: Ten-million-year-old hominid apes are known from East Africa: Chororapithecus from Ethiopia's Afar rift, and Nakalipithecus. They date from about the time the gorilla branch split from the branch leading to humans and chimpanzees, around 10 Ma.

mioc-122.title: The Pannonian Sea is cut off
mioc-122.text: Around 10 Ma the Carpathians rose. Their uplift isolated the Pannonian Sea from the rest of the Paratethys, another step in the breakup of the old inland sea.

mioc-124.title: The Rivera microplate breaks away
mioc-124.text: Plates can split into smaller pieces. Around 10 Ma, off western Mexico, the Rivera plate broke away from the Cocos plate. It became a microplate, a small independent slab of crust with its own motion.

mioc-119.title: Baja California tears away from Mexico
mioc-119.text: Rifting began opening the Gulf of California 10–6 Ma, tearing the Baja California peninsula northwest from mainland Mexico. Geologists widely date the gulf itself to around 5.3 million years ago, when the rift tore Baja California off the North American plate. The East Pacific Rise, a mid-ocean spreading ridge, pushed up the middle of the gulf, forming the Gulf of California Rift Zone. The new gulf changed the rivers around it. Its opening around 6 Ma let a large river cut its way northeast, and by 5.5–5 Ma streams there had merged into one major river, the subject of {{ref:plio-010}}.

mioc-115.title: The Altiplano–Puna ignimbrite flare-up
mioc-115.text: About 10,000 km³ of ignimbrite erupted from the Altiplano–Puna volcanic complex between 10 and 1 Ma, over crust 70 km thick. It began from below. Mafic magma, rich in iron and magnesium, was injected into the lower crust, and an overturn before 10.6 Ma melted crust and started the eruptions. From about 10 Ma the calderas erupted in four pulses separated by quieter spells. Volcanism peaked 8–4 Ma with huge eruptions at Cerro Panizos, Coranzulí, Vilama, Cerro Guacha and La Pacana.

mioc-125.title: Livyatan, the sperm whale with giant teeth
mioc-125.text: Livyatan had the largest biting teeth known. This 13.5–17.5 m sperm whale hunted off Peru 9.9–8.9 Ma. Teeth from Chile to Australia suggest it or a close relative ranged widely and survived to about 5 Ma. End-Miocene cooling probably shrank its food supply and caused its extinction.

mioc-126.title: Oreodonts fade as deer and bovids arrive
mioc-126.text: North America's cast of mammals changed in the Hemphillian age, from about 9.4 Ma. The last oreodonts, mylagaulids and dromomerycids died out. Newcomers walked in from Asia: deer, bovids, saber-toothed cats and skunks. At home, rabbits and short-faced bears diversified.

mioc-127.title: Asia's winter monsoons grow stronger
mioc-127.text: Monsoons blow both ways, wet in summer and dry and cold in winter. The South Asian winter monsoon strengthened about 9.2–8.5 Ma. From 7.9 to 5.8 Ma, the East Asian winter monsoon also grew stronger, as the subarctic front, the boundary of cold northern air, shifted south. Around 5.5 Ma the East Asian winter monsoon intensified rapidly.

mioc-129.title: Cerro Ballena's whale graveyard
mioc-129.text: In Chile's Atacama Desert lie over 40 whales, along with seals, sailfish, swordfish, sharks and aquatic sloths. They died in four separate mass deaths. Toxic algal blooms, fed by high iron levels, likely poisoned them before waves washed the carcasses ashore.

mioc-131.title: Gargano's fissure traps
mioc-131.text: On Gargano in Italy, cracks opened in old Jurassic rock. Miocene mammals and birds fell into these fissures and were buried. Over time they built up large deposits of well-preserved animals. The cracks worked as natural pitfall traps.

mioc-133.title: The Lake Malawi basin begins to form
mioc-133.text: The Lake Malawi basin began forming about 8.6 Ma, far earlier than once thought. Water came much later. Deep water first appeared there only 4.5 Ma, millions of years after the basin itself opened in the rift.

mioc-134.title: Vilama's VEI 8 supereruption
mioc-134.text: Vilama caldera in the Andes erupted the enormous Vilama ignimbrite about 8.5–8.4 Ma, a VEI 8 eruption at the top of the volcanic scale. The 1,000 km³ Sifon ignimbrite, erupted 8.33 Ma, may also have come from Vilama.

mioc-136.title: Graecopithecus and Ouranopithecus in Europe
mioc-136.text: Apes from Greece and Anatolia, Graecopithecus and Ouranopithecus, date to about 8 Ma. Some have taken them as a sign that hominins spread beyond Africa early. They are probably members of Homininae, the African great-ape subfamily, but not of the human tribe, Hominini.

mioc-139.title: The Leporid Datum: rabbits and hares everywhere
mioc-139.text: Around 8 Ma, rabbits and hares abruptly diversified and spread across the Northern Hemisphere. The event is sudden and widespread enough to serve as a marker in the rock record, called the Leporid Datum. The spread kept going. By 7 Ma the group had expanded into South America and Africa.

mioc-138.title: The world dries out
mioc-138.text: A colder atmosphere holds less moisture. As the globe cooled, the air dried, driving a worldwide trend toward aridity, especially after 8–7 Ma. The effects showed everywhere. Uplift of East Africa helped shrink its rainforests. Australia dried as it drifted into a low-rainfall zone, though its southwest grew wetter 12–8 Ma. The Tian Shan blocked westerly winds and dried the Tarim Basin. In Kenya's Great Rift Valley aridity rose gradually, with wet spells still returning. One theory links the Sahara's drying to a monsoon weakened when the Tethys Sea dried up around 7 Ma.

openers.late-miocene: About 11 million years ago the Middle Miocene Warm Interval ended, and the much cooler Late Miocene Cool Interval began. The cold reshaped life on every continent. Europe's large mammal diversity fell, and South America's giant crocodilians and native predators faded as wetlands vanished. Off southwest Africa, the cold Benguela Upwelling began. Meanwhile the land kept changing: the modern Yangtze River took shape, and Andean calderas such as Aguas Calientes poured out vast ignimbrites.
